 High price, short supply leave LPG consumers in trouble
 Lahore 
 By   Munawar Hasan 
 November 08, 2026 
 A motorised auto-rickshaw powered by liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) passes a bridge amid rising fuel and LPG prices due to the Iran conflict, in Karachi, Pakistan, September 11, 2026. — Reuters  LAHORE : Prices and supplies of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) are under unprecedented pressure amid high winter demand, leaving hapless consumers to contend with higher costs and limited availability.
 Households that rely on LPG for cooking are entering winter amid a familiar squeeze: the regulator’s announced price and the amount consumers actually pay have diverged sharply, with the gap widening as demand started to peak. For November, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority set the official LPG price at Rs294.07 per kg, equivalent to Rs3,470.09 for a standard 11.8-kg domestic cylinder. Retail prices, however, are reported at Rs 520 to Rs 600 per kg in major cities and as high as Rs630 to Rs700 in some parts of the country. In the provincial metropolis, LPG prices hover around Rs600 to Rs700 per kg, while residents also report supply shortages.
 For many households, this has made cooking gas availability and soaring prices a source of anxiety, as retail cylinder prices climb to Rs6,000 to Rs7,200—roughly twice the notified rate.
 The impact is greatest on families without access to piped gas, as well as those receiving little or no supply through the piped network. In these difficult circumstances, LPG—once dubbed the ‘poor man’s fuel’—is no longer an affordable or accessible option for many.
 Hotels, restaurants and small food businesses also depend on the same cylinder supply, and their higher costs are ultimately passed on to consumers.
 The pressure is no longer merely seasonal. This year, the usual increase in demand has coincided with supply complications linked to border-trade disruptions and volatility in international markets amid uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz. Every delay in import arrivals further tightens retail availability and pushes prices higher.
 A framework announced after the federal cabinet meeting could affect consumers, though key details remain unclear. Public-sector entities will play a greater role in LPG imports, but it is uncertain whether state importers can secure enough supply at competitive rates amid peak winter demand and disrupted supply lines. Initial cargoes may be delayed, while marketing companies’ inventories are at record lows.
 If imports fall short before or during December and January, retail availability could tighten and prices rise sharply. With global prices high and supplies constrained, retail rates are likely to remain above notified levels unless competitively priced LPG becomes more available.
 Under the new arrangements, state-owned companies will receive 10 percent of LPG production at a different price from private buyers, creating two cost bases in one market. A fund for low-income consumers has also been announced, but how it will be funded and disbursed—and whether it will link to programmes such as BISP—remains unclear.
 The framework also introduces auctions of LPG in small lots, a practice producers have followed since 2007. In the coming weeks, market sentiment will depend on import arrivals, domestic supply and enforcement of notified prices at the point of sale. With inventories exceptionally low, households preparing winter budgets may pay well above the official rate.
 The News contacted Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik for comment on the expanded role of public-sector entities in imports and the proposed fund, financed through the price differential. He was asked to clarify the timeline for additional imported volumes, how notified prices would be enforced at the point of sale, what contingency measures would apply if spot prices remained high, and how a level playing field would be ensured for public and private marketers sourcing from the same fields. Until these questions are answered on the record, the notified price remains an announcement rather than a practical reality. The minister was unavailable for the comment.
